entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12121"/><div sID="gen21943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12121"/><hi type="bold">9. little horn--</hi>not to be confounded with the little horn of the fourth kingdom in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>. The little horn in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference> comes as an eleventh horn after ten preceding horns. In <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference> it is not an independent fifth horn, after the four previous ones, but it arises out of one of the four existing horns. This horn is explained (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Da 8:23</reference>) to be "a king of fierce countenance," &c. Antiochus Epiphanes is meant. Greece with all its refinement produces the first, that is, the Old Testament Antichrist. Antiochus had an extraordinary love of art, which expressed itself in grand temples. He wished to substitute Zeus Olympius for Jehovah at Jerusalem. Thus first heathen civilization from below, and revealed religion from above, came into collision. Identifying himself with Jupiter, his aim was to make his own worship universal (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">Da 8:25</reference> with <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>); so mad was he in this that he was called Epimanes (maniac) instead of Epiphanes. None of the previous world rulers, Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.31-Dan.4.34">Da 4:31-34</reference>), Darius (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.27">Da 6:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.28">28</reference>), Cyrus (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.2-Ezra.1.4">Ezr 1:2-4</reference>), Artaxerxes Longimanus (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.12">Ezr 7:12</reference>), had systematically opposed the Jews' religious worship. Hence the need of prophecy to prepare them for Antiochus. The struggle of the Maccabees was a fruit of Daniel's prophecy (1 Maccabees 2:59). He is the forerunner of the final Antichrist, standing in the same relation to the first advent of Christ that Antichrist does to His second coming. The sins in Israel which gave rise to the Greek Antichrist were that some Jews adopted Hellenic customs (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Da 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">32</reference>), erecting theaters, and regarding all religions alike, sacrificing to Jehovah, but at the same time sending money for sacrifices to Hercules. Such shall be the state of the world when ripe for Antichrist. At <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Da 8:23</reference> the description passes from the literal Antiochus to features which, though partially attributed to him, hold good in their fullest sense only of his antitype, the New Testament Antichrist. The Mohammedan Antichrist may also be included; answering to the Euphratean (Turk) horsemen (<reference osisRef="Rev.9.14-Rev.9.21">Re 9:14-21</reference>), loosed "an hour, a day, a month, a year" (391 years, in the year-day theory), to scourge corrupted, idolatrous Christianity. In A.D. 637 the Saracen Moslem mosque of Omar was founded on the site of the temple, "treading under foot the sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.11-Dan.8.13">Da 8:11-13</reference>); and there it still remains. The first conquest of the Turks over Christians was in A.D. 1281; and 391 years after they reached their zenith of power and began to decline, Sobieski defeating them at Vienna. Mohammed II, called "the conqueror," reigned A.D. 1451-1481, in which period Constantinople fell; 391 years after brings us to our own day, in which Turkey's fall is imminent.<div eID="gen21943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waxed ... great, toward ... south--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.11.25">Da 11:25</reference>). Antiochus fought against Ptolemy Philometer and Egypt, that is, the south.<div eID="gen21944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward the east--</hi>He fought against those who attempted a change of government in Persia.<div eID="gen21945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward the pleasant land--</hi>Judea, "the glorious land" (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Da 11:16</reference>, 41, 45; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.15">15</reference>). Its chief pleasantness consists in its being God's chosen land (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">Psa 132:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jr 3:19</reference>). Into it Antiochus made his inroad after his return from Egypt. <div eID="gen21946" type="x-p"/>

Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.1.5">Ge 1:5</reference>. Six years and a hundred ten days. This includes not only the three and a half years during which the daily sacrifice was forbidden by Antiochus [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 1:1.1], but the whole series of events whereby it was practically interrupted: beginning with the "little horn waxing great toward the pleasant land," and "casting down some of the host" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">10</reference>); namely, when in 171 B.C., or the month Sivan in the year 142 of the era of the Seleucidæ, the sacrifices began to be neglected, owing to the high priest Jason introducing at Jerusalem Grecian customs and amusements, the palæstra and gymnasium; ending with the death of Antiochus, 165 B.C., or the month Shebath, in the year 148 of the Seleucid era. Compare 1 Maccabees 1:11-15; 2 Maccabees 4:9, &c. The reason for the greater minuteness of historical facts and dates, given in Daniel's prophecies, than in those of the New Testament, is that Israel, not having yet the clear views which Christians have of immortality and the heavenly inheritance, could only be directed to the earthly future: for it was on earth the looked-for Messiah was to appear, and the sum and subject of Old Testament prophecy was the kingdom of God upon earth. The minuteness of the revelation of Israel's earthly destiny was to compensate for the absence, in the Old Testament, of views of heavenly glory. Thus, in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Da 9:24-27</reference>, the times of Messiah are foretold to the very year; in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Da 8:14</reference> the times of Antiochus, even to the day; and in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.5-Dan.11.20">Da 11:5-20</reference> the Syro-Egyptian struggles in most minute detail. The event, however, may, in the case of Antichrist, show a correspondence between the days here given and <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>, such as is not yet discernible. The term of twenty-three hundred days cannot refer twenty-three hundred years of the treading down of Christianity by Mohammedanism, as this would leave the greater portion of the time yet future; whereas, Mohammedanism is fast waning. Cumming remarks, 480 B.C. is the date of the waning of the Persian empire before Greece; deducting 480 from 2300, we have 1820; and in 1821, Turkey, the successor of the Greek empire, began to wane, and Greece became a separate kingdom. See on Da 12:11 . cleansed-- literally, "justified," vindicated from profanation. Judas Maccabeus celebrated the feast of dedication after the cleansing, on the twenty-fifth of the ninth month, Kisleu (1 Maccabees 4:51-58; 2 Maccabees 10:1-7; Joh 10:22 ). As to the antitypical dedication of the new temple, see Eze 43:1-27 , &c.; also Am 9:11 , 12 .

The event being to take place at "the time of the end" makes it likely that the Antichrist ultimately referred to (besides the immediate reference to Antiochus) in this chapter, and the one in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>, are one and the same. The objection that the one in the seventh chapter springs out of the ten divisions of the Roman earth, the fourth kingdom, the one in the eighth chapter and the eleventh chapter from one of the four divisions of the third kingdom, Greece, is answered thus: The four divisions of the Grecian empire, having become parts of the Roman empire, shall at the end form four of its ten final divisions [Tregelles]. However, the origin from one of the four parts of the third kingdom may be limited to Antiochus, the immediate subject of the eighth and eleventh chapter, while the ulterior typical reference of these chapters (namely, Antichrist) may belong to one of the ten Roman divisions, not necessarily one formerly of the four of the third kingdom. The event will tell. "Time of the end" may apply to the time of Antiochus. For it is the prophetic phrase for the time of fulfilment, seen always at the end of the prophetic horizon (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.1">Ge 49:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.14">Nu 24:14</reference>). <div eID="gen21965" type="x-p"/>
